reason: The judgment construes Rent Act section 22 and holds that single-house ownership is not a condition precedent to this ejectment action.
The court described the protection for a tenant against a purchaser-over-the-head but held it did not apply because the plaintiff was already the landlord before purchase.
The court relied on the omission from the Praveni list, absent adequate explanation, to infer Maruwena tenure and uphold the temple trustee's superior title.
The decisive holding was that the evidence did not establish collusion within section 7(2) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
The statement overgeneralises the exceptio rei venditae et traditae holding and omits the prior transfer and later reacquisition facts that made title pass to Swarna Jayanthi.
The court held that recalling probate could not rest on an unsupported finding that the appellant did not understand Sinhala.
The court held that time generally runs on each overdraft when made and that the dormant overdraft claim against the customer was prescribed.
The section 68 point was framed as an alternative after the court said due execution had not arisen at trial, and the statement omits the notary-dead and witness context.
The jurisdiction holding was confined to the borrower's challenge to the Bank's mortgage-sale purchase and is too broad without that context.
The court directly construed section 50(1) to bar post-mortgage claimants through the borrower, while preserving the borrower's own challenge.
The statement omits the material qualification that the certificate does not prevent review of whether the Bank acted lawfully, in good faith, and commercially reasonably.
The quoted purchaser-standing proposition was noted as settled and undisputed, while the appeal turned on the absence of proof that the management document was a sham subletting.
The court's operative factual holding was that no evidence showed document IV 10 was a sham rather than the management agreement it purported to be.
The Supreme Court ordered a fresh trial because the District Judge's misunderstanding of the primary land-use facts vitiated the judgment.
The statement states the section 2 rule but drops the central fraud exception under which the court considered the non-notarial document.
The court held that abandonment of a lawful Viharadhipathi's right is strongly presumed against and must be clearly proved.
The court's holding was that this was not a section 7 money-lent or account-stated claim but a mortgage-bond claim governed by section 5.
The court upheld adding the finance company as a defendant to avoid multiplicity and fully adjudicate the alleged fraudulent title transaction.
The court held that failure to submit the local-agent registration required by Clause 29 before bidding made the tender board's acceptance unlawful.
The court held that Clause 13 required rejection of a bid lacking acceptable bid security for the required period.
The court held that failure to notify all tenderers and invite representations breached Guideline 136 and violated equal-opportunity transparency.
The court affirmed revocation of deed P3 because the donee wife's conduct amounted to ingratitude on the facts found.
The statement reverses the holding, because the court held the relief was not prescribed despite the lapse of more than ten years.
The court held that once deed P3 was revoked, the plaintiff's later gift of the same property to her nephews was null and void.
The court held that an intestate's rights vested immediately in the heirs and that those vested rights could be validly gifted by notarial deed.
